title: The System Design Interview
objectives: Explain The System Design Interview with measurable requirements and failure modes
A 45-minute collaborative conversation where you clarify, estimate, sketch, and defend trade-offs.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Interviewers grade how you think, not a single right diagram. They watch for: clarifying scope, sensible numbers, a clean high-level design, a deep dive into one hard part, and honest trade-offs.

cards.title: diagram
cards.body:

cards.title: text
cards.body: Jumping straight into Kafka and microservices before asking what the product does. Always spend the first 5 minutes on requirements.

title: Back-of-Envelope Estimation
objectives: Explain Back-of-Envelope Estimation with measurable requirements and failure modes
Turn users into QPS, storage and bandwidth with rounded math: 1 day ≈ 10^5 seconds.

cards.title: text
cards.body: QPS = DAU × actions per user ÷ 86,400. Peak ≈ 2–10× average. Storage = writes/day × object size × retention. Round aggressively; the order of magnitude matters.

title: Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal + Load Balancers
objectives: Explain Scaling: Vertical vs Horizontal + Load Balancers with measurable requirements and failure modes
Scale up with a bigger box or scale out with more boxes behind a load balancer.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Vertical scaling is simple but hits a ceiling and is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling needs stateless services, a load balancer and partitioned data, but grows almost linearly.

title: TCP vs UDP
objectives: Explain TCP vs UDP with measurable requirements and failure modes
HTTP is request/response over TCP; HTTPS adds TLS for encryption, integrity and server identity.

cards.title: text
cards.body: TLS handshake negotiates keys using certificates. HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reuses connections, HTTP/2 multiplexes streams, HTTP/3 runs on QUIC (UDP) to avoid head-of-line blocking.

cards.title: text
cards.body: HTTP is request/response over TCP; HTTPS adds TLS for encryption, integrity and server identity.

cards.title: diagram
cards.body:
Step through how a request moves.

Flow: TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → Server processes → HTTP response

cards.title: text
cards.body: Terminating TLS on every microservice without reason. Usually TLS ends at the edge/LB and mTLS is used internally only when needed.

cards.body: Close by restating scope, numbers, and the main risk for TCP vs UDP. HTTP is request/response over TCP; HTTPS adds TLS for encryption, integrity and server identity.

title: DNS
objectives: Explain DNS with measurable requirements and failure modes
DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Browsers ask a recursive resolver, which walks root → .in/.com TLD → authoritative server and caches by TTL. Low TTLs allow fast failover; high TTLs reduce lookups.

cards.title: text
cards.body: DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.

cards.title: diagram
cards.body:
Step through how a request moves.

Flow: Browser cache → Recursive resolver → Root server → TLD (.in) → Authoritative → IP

cards.title: text
cards.body: Forgetting that DNS caching delays failover. A 24 h TTL means some users hit the dead region for a day.

cards.title: animation
cards.body: Close by restating scope, numbers, and the main risk for DNS. DNS maps names to IPs through a cached hierarchy: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative.

title: Forward vs Reverse Proxy
objectives: Explain Forward vs Reverse Proxy with measurable requirements and failure modes
A reverse proxy fronts servers (TLS, caching, compression); a forward proxy fronts clients.

title: Stateless Services & Sessions

A load balancer spreads traffic across healthy instances and removes failed ones.

cards.title: text
cards.body: LBs sit in front of a pool, run health checks, and route each request to a healthy backend. They enable horizontal scaling and zero-downtime deploys by draining instances.

title: Where to Cache
objectives: Explain Where to Cache with measurable requirements and failure modes
Caches keep hot data in fast storage to cut latency and offload databases.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Reads often follow a power law: a small set of keys gets most traffic. Serving them from memory (Redis, local LRU) drops latency from ms to µs and shields the DB.

title: Cache Strategies
objectives: Explain Cache Strategies with measurable requirements and failure modes
Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Cache-aside: app reads cache, on miss reads DB and sets cache. Write-through: write cache and DB synchronously (fresh, slower writes). Write-behind: write cache, flush DB later (fast, risk of loss).

cards.title: text
cards.body: Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Using write-behind for payments. Losing buffered writes on a crash is unacceptable for money.

cards.title: animation
cards.body: Close by restating scope, numbers, and the main risk for Cache Strategies. Cache-aside loads on miss; write-through writes both; write-behind writes cache then DB asynchronously.

title: Eviction Policies
objectives: Explain Eviction Policies with measurable requirements and failure modes
When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

cards.title: text
cards.body: LRU evicts least recently used — good default. LFU keeps frequently used items — good for stable hot sets. TTL expires data by age regardless of use.

cards.title: text
cards.body: When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

cards.title: text

cards.title: animation
cards.body: Close by restating scope, numbers, and the main risk for Eviction Policies. When memory is full: LRU, LFU, FIFO or TTL decide what to drop.

title: Redis Deep Dive

Shared in-memory caches scale out across nodes using sharding and replication.

cards.title: text
cards.body: Redis offers data structures (sorted sets, hashes), persistence, replication and cluster sharding. Memcached is simple, multithreaded key-value. Clients shard keys with consistent hashing.
